synthesis.answer:
Most of the regularity comes from arithmetic, not from a smooth law. The top edge does follow a simple curve, d_max ≈ 0.617·√(n ln n), but the data cannot pick that curve over several others, and no theorem selects it.

Three sources of regularity have nothing to do with a function. First, d is always even (proved), so the 533 entries use only 14 heights and land on just 221 distinct (n, d) points. Second, for lm ≤ 200 criterion E reduces to "lm divisible by 3, 7, 31, 73 or 85". Codes therefore exist at only 89 of the 153 possible n, and 65 of those are every multiple of 6 from 12 to 396, so the x-axis is close to an evenly spaced comb. Third, 209 of the 533 entries (39%) come from isomorphic tori and sit exactly on top of other points.

The top of every column is the smallest k its group allows (141 of 141 groups): k = 4 when 3 divides n/2, 6 when only 7 does, and 10, 16 or 18 for 31, 85 or 73. So the upper edge is one k = 4 staircase on the multiples of 6. It rises by 2 at each new even level and dips once, at n = 312. The other columns sit 0 to 16 below it.

Below the edge the k layers run roughly parallel. At fixed n, each extra logical qubit costs about one unit of distance: the median slope within a group is 0.91, drifting from about 0.7 at n ≤ 150 to about 1.25 above n = 300. Fitted only on n ≤ 300, d ≈ 2.31·n^0.443 − k predicts the 49 stage-4 frontier points with RMS 2.0 to 2.1, with 92 to 94% within one even step. The k·d² ≈ constant shape does much worse (RMS 3.7). The apparent ceiling of about 14 to 16 on k·d²/n is not real. The best score for each k still rises from band to band (k = 10 goes 4.3 → 15.6). The published [[360,12,24]] sits on Z6×Z30, which stage 4 has not computed yet, so the (360, 12) entry must rise to d ≥ 24, a score of 19.2.

On the top edge, d/√n at each new record rises at every step, from 1.155 at [[48,4,8]] to 1.488 at [[354,4,28]], so a constant ratio is ruled out. The tightest constant line, 1.46·√n (through [[270,4,24]]), falls about 0.6 short at the d = 26 and d = 28 steps. √n·ln n and a straight line overshoot.

The best simple description is d_max ≈ 0.617·√(n ln n), rounded down to even. But over n ≤ 400 it stays within 0.35 in d of 0.83·n^0.60 and 0.78·n^0.613. The form 1.75·√n − 4.6, in which d/√n levels off near 1.75, fits as well once the small-n steps are dropped. It is clearly worse only when they are kept (ΔAICc ≈ 12 from n ≥ 30). So the data say only that the edge grows faster than √n here, with a local exponent of about 0.6.

Out of sample, 0.615·√(n ln n) fitted on n ≤ 300 gets the record value right at 13 of the 14 stage-4 n where a record is set (14 of all 20 stage-4 n). Because d is even, that is really only two events. It placed d = 28 at n ≈ 353 (first seen at 354) and missed d = 26 (predicted at 311, seen at 306, the same point where the registered 0.801·n^0.607 failed by 0.1). One hit in two matches its in-sample rate (it misses 4 of its 10 training steps), and n^0.60 scores the same 13/14. The √(n ln n) form was also chosen after stage 4 was visible, so only its constant was really tested.

The edge is also a maximum over many code classes: only 1 to 5 classes hold each new record. The bulk of classes rises nearly as fast (mean, median and 90th percentile grow like n^0.68 to n^0.71 for n ≤ 198). But the best of a fixed-size sample grows like n^0.63, against n^0.67 for the real maximum. Classes per n grow about like n^2.7, and that alone is worth about one even step across the range. Any fitted curve absorbs this effect.

Theory does not fix the shape. The best proven upper bound for weight-6 BB codes, and for any abelian two-block code, is O(n^(3/4)), from a Bravyi–Terhal argument in 4 dimensions (Arnault, Gaborit, Rozendaal, Saussay, Zémor, arXiv:2502.04995; Postema & Kokkelmans, arXiv:2502.17052). Its explicit form, about 8.5·n^(3/4), holds only for n ≥ 16,384 and says nothing here. Caps of order √n are proven only for subfamilies that exclude the record codes: hypergraph products (Tillich–Zémor, arXiv:0903.0566) and codes whose A or B lies in a small subgroup (Lin–Pryadko, arXiv:2306.16400). Wang & Pryadko (arXiv:2203.17216) prove that codes with d of order √n exist at fixed weight, and found that A√n + B fits their k = 2 enumerations. So theory allows exponents from 1/2 to 3/4, and the observed ≈0.6 lies inside that window. Up to n = 384 the record codes can be drawn as 2D codes with small stencils (diameter ≤ 3, occasionally 4). So 2D bounds such as Bravyi–Poulin–Terhal's k·d² = O(n) apply, but their constants are unknown, so they do not predict the numbers. The literature was checked only through search summaries, because arxiv.org was blocked.

Several things are not established. The range stops at n = 384, and stage 4 is about 75% done: n = 360 and 384 are missing groups, and n = 390 to 396 have not run. The whole edge rests on about 12 step positions, each known only to within 6 in n, and one step of 2 is 7% of d at d = 28. The leading forms separate by one even step only at n ≈ 530 to 1500 (power law against the rest), n ≈ 1000 to 2000 (√(n ln n) against A√n + B), and n of order 10^4 (the log-corrected forms against each other).
synthesis.formula:
**Top edge (record staircase; k = 4 codes on n divisible by 6):**
- d_max(n) ≈ 2·floor(0.617·√(n·ln n) / 2).
- c = 0.617 is fitted to all 12 record steps (d = 6 to 28, n ≤ 384). Fitting n ≤ 300 only gives 0.615. Single steps give values from 0.603 to 0.625, and no single c fits all of them.
- Over 30 ≤ n ≤ 400 these are equally good and within about 0.35 in d of each other: 0.78·n^0.613 (≈ 0.83·n^0.60), √n·(ln n)^0.55, and, if the fit starts at n ≳ 90, 1.75·√n − 4.6.
- Ruled out: c·√n (tightest constant 1.46, falls about 0.6 short by n = 306 to 354), c·√n·ln n, and a + b·n.
- Valid only for 30 ≤ n ≤ ~400 and only for the top edge. Columns where only 7 divides n/2 sit 0 to 2 lower; columns set by 31, 85 or 73 sit 4 to 16 lower.
- Do not extrapolate: at n = 10^4 the forms predict d/√n between 1.63 and 2.20.

**k layers below the edge:**
- d_best(n, k) ≈ 2.31·n^0.443 − k, fitted on n ≤ 300; 1.71·√n − k does about as well.
- Accuracy: about ±2 (one even step) for 92 to 94% of points, for k ≤ 16 and n ≤ 400.
- The cost per unit of k drifts from about 0.7 to about 1 as n grows.
- It fails for k ≥ 18, and for gross-type k = 12 codes (groups with two even sides and a Z3×Z3 part), which sit 1 to 2.5 steps above it.

**Arithmetic skeleton (exact, not a fit):**
- d is even.
- For lm ≤ 200, codes exist exactly when lm is divisible by 3, 7, 31, 73 or 85.
- The k at a column's top is 2·ord_t(2): 4, 6, 10, 16 or 18.
synthesis.next_test:
**Prediction to register before running (a targeted stage 5, not a full census).** Run k = 4 codes on the 3×m tori with m = 130 to 134, i.e. n = 780, 786, 792, 798, 804. These are all cyclic or near-cyclic groups with k = 4, the same family that holds every record so far. Record the best distance in that band. Fitted on all 12 record steps, the candidates predict:

| Model | Value at n = 804 | Predicted band maximum |
|---|---|---|
| Power law 0.78·n^0.613 | 46.9 | 46 |
| 0.617·√(n ln n) | 45.2 | 44 |
| A√n + B, 1.66√n − 3.3 | 43.8 | 42 |
| A√n + B, 1.75√n − 4.6 | 44.9 | 44 |
| Constant ratio c√n | 40.2 to 40.9 | 40 |

How to read the result:
- 46 or more favours the power law.
- 44 fits √(n ln n), or A√n + B fitted from n ≥ 100.
- 42 or less refutes both the power law and the √(n ln n) envelope, and favours d/√n levelling off.
- One-step misses happen (the √(n ln n) envelope misses 4 of its 10 in-sample steps), so only a two-step outcome (≤ 42 or ≥ 48) would be strong evidence.
- Separating √(n ln n) from A√n + B needs n ≈ 1000 to 2000.

**Feasibility.** Certifying d ≈ 46 exactly is beyond current tools: a d = 30 class already needs about 1.5 days against a 4-hour limit. So register the test in an asymmetric form:
- Cheap window upper bounds on every class in the band cap the true maximum. A largest upper bound of 44 or less refutes the power law; 42 or less also refutes √(n ln n).
- Refuting the lower curves needs one code certified at d ≥ 46.

**Stage 4's remaining tori cannot decide this.** These are n = 384 (Z4×Z48, Z8×Z24), 390 (Z195), 392 and 396. Every candidate predicts d = 28 at n = 384 and a first d = 30 somewhere between n = 390 and 402. A certified d = 30 at n = 390 would lean weakly toward the power law, and d = 30 may not be certifiable within the time limit anyway. Stage 4 will settle one thing: computing 6×30 must lift the (360, 12) entry to d ≥ 24 (score 19.2). That follows from the published code, so it is not a test.

synthesis.dropped_claims:
**Envelope**
- "0.615·√(n ln n) gets 13 of 14 stage-4 records exact" is reframed. Because d is even, that is 1 hit in 2 transitions (it misses d = 26 at 306 and hits d = 28 at 354). That matches its in-sample rate (it misses 4 of its 10 training steps). n^0.60 also scores 13/14, and the form was chosen after stage 4 was visible.
- "c·√n comes out a full even step too low" is replaced. The tightest constant (1.46) misses by about 0.6 and gets 10/14 exact. The −1.9 to −2.1 figure is mostly the model's misfit inside the training range, carried forward.
- c·√n·(1 − e^(−n/n0)) is not robustly ruled out: fitted on n = 200 to 300 it gets 13/14.
- "A√n + B cannot be separated" is corrected. Fitted from n ≥ 30 it is disfavoured (ΔAICc ≈ 12.4). It ties only once the fit starts at n ≳ 90.
- "Forms separate at n ≈ 630 to 1700" is corrected. The range runs from about 530 to about 20,000 depending on the pair, and the two-parameter log-corrected forms need n of order 10^4.
- "√(n ln n) and n^0.61 to 0.64 have the same shape within 1.7%" is corrected. That holds only for b ≈ 0.60 to 0.61. b = 0.64 is wrong at 10 of 79 n.
- "The two leading forms separate by one step around n ≈ 1000" is corrected to about n ≈ 620 to 750 (two steps at 1000).
- The 60/63 staircase match is in-sample only. The constant was tuned to a window of 0.6173 to 0.6181, and n^0.6 and the registered law also score 60/63.

**Extreme values**
- "The edge is a sharp cutoff, not an extreme-value lottery" and "class count is worth at most 0.5 in d" are dropped. The data cannot tell a cutoff from a lottery. Class count is worth about 1 to 2 in d across the range. The within-n pair result (3 higher / 12 equal / 1 lower) is what a pure lottery would also produce. The evt.py counts at d_max − 2 for the stage-3d tori were really counts at d_max − 4.
- "The rise of d/√n is not an extreme-value effect" is softened. The bulk of classes does rise, but about 20% of the maximum's extra exponent above 1/2 (0.67 against 0.63 for a fixed sample size) comes from the growing class count. Requiring at least 3 classes at the band maxima lowers them by about one step (1.265/1.333/1.389 become 1.231/1.306/1.342). The Gaussian benchmark is 2.67, not 3.19.

**k trade-off**
- "1.692·√n − k reproduces all eight band maxima within 0.03" is dropped. The first band misses by 0.040. All the band maxima are k = 4 codes, so they never test the −k term, and the agreement comes from errors cancelling. With a constant c the model is misspecified for k ≥ 6.
- "d + k is nearly constant" is softened. It holds only to within 1 to 2 even steps (median spread 4). The slope drifts with n, and a linear fall in k cannot be told apart from D(1 − k/28) or D·e^(−k/15).
- "Best k·d²/n is bounded at about 14 to 16" is dropped. It is still rising, and the uncomputed Z6×Z30 holds [[360,12,24]], which scores 19.2.

**Theory**
- "The best codes are not a fixed-stencil 2D-local family; the stencil grows like N^(1/4); BPT does not apply" is dropped. The minimal stencil levels off at diameter 3 for n = 200 to 384, so 2D bounds apply within the range, with unknown constants.
- "√n is proven only for hypergraph products" is corrected. Lin–Pryadko's bound d ≤ min(|G_a|, |G_b|) also gives √n for other subfamilies, though not for the record codes.
- The n^(3/4) bound's n counts group elements, so in census units it reads 8.49·n^(3/4), valid for n ≥ 16,384.

**Structure**
- The single-frontier-point rule holds on all census groups but is not a general iff (Z5×Z85 is a counterexample).
- The cyclic group's advantage at the column top is not fully explained by its larger class count (stratified test at n ≤ 200, P < 1e-4).

angles.summary: Yes, there is a simple function that describes the top edge of the d-vs-n plot well, but the data cannot tell which kind of function is the right one. One parameter is enough: d_max(n) ≈ 0.62·sqrt(n·ln n). Over n = 30 to 384 this curve is nearly the same as 0.78·n^0.61 and as 1.66·sqrt(n) − 3.3. Each even d first appears within about one n-step (about 6) of where the curve crosses d. I fitted it only on n ≤ 300 (stages 3a and 3b/3c) and rounded down to even. On stage 4 it gave exactly the right value at 13 of the 14 n where the record is reached. It also placed d = 28 at n ≈ 353, and d = 28 was in fact first seen at 354. The data clearly rule out a constant d/sqrt(n): fitted on n ≤ 300, c·sqrt(n) comes out about one full even step (≈ 2) too low on stage 4 and is wrong at 0 of 14. They also rule out sqrt(n)·ln n and a straight line (too high), and the form c·sqrt(n)(1 − e^(−n/n0)). They do not separate sqrt(n ln n), n^0.61, sqrt(n)(ln n)^0.55, sqrt(n)(a + b·sqrt(ln n)) and A·sqrt(n) + B. Which of these wins on information criteria flips depending on where the fit starts (n ≥ 30 or n ≥ 100). Telling them apart needs censuses up to n ≈ 1000 to 2000 (d ≈ 50 to 70), which is far beyond what exact distances can currently reach. Part of why the plot looks regular has nothing to do with a function: d comes only in even values, n only takes certain values, and the few n with only a handful of classes sit below the edge. The top edge also behaves like a sharp cutoff, not like a lottery over many codes. Only 1 to a few dozen classes hold the top value at each n, against hundreds or thousands at d − 2. Once a group has more than about 1000 classes, having more classes barely raises the maximum. The registered power law failed at n = 306 by a tiny margin (f(306) = 25.9 against d = 26). Almost every good smooth fit misses that point the same way, so a hard "round down to even" envelope is too strict a test.

- E(n): the largest settled d at each n, over all tori and all k.
- R(n): the running maximum of E, i.e. the staircase.
- On the staircase means E = R.
- n_first(d): the first n with E ≥ d. The crossing point n_x is taken halfway between n_first and the previous n that has codes.
- First appearances (d:n): 4:18, 6:30, 8:48, 10:66, 12:90, 14:114, 16:144, 18:168, 20:204, 22:234, 24:270 | stage 4: 26:306, 28:354.

- The edge is almost always a k = 4 code on a torus with 3 | l (n = 6m). The k = 6 codes on 7-type tori run about 0.1 lower in d/sqrt(n).

angles.caveats:
- **Coverage.** n only reaches 384, which is less than a factor of 13 above n = 30. Stage 4 is about 75% done. The test set has 20 n with codes (14 on the staircase) and only two new even levels (26 and 28). Out of sample, the result is tested mainly by those two crossing points.
- **Even steps.** One step of 2 in d is about 7% here, so the strict "round down to even" test can be failed by a 0.1 miss (that is what happened to the registered law at n = 306). The crossing-point fits handle the steps, but their residuals still depend on where codes happen to exist in n (about every 6 near the edge).
- **The noise model is not realistic.** The model ranking (AICc, BIC) and the simulated censuses assume independent Gaussian errors. Crossing points share structure from number theory and from which groups exist. MID points are strongly autocorrelated, so their information-criterion gaps are overstated. The "n needed to tell them apart" figures assume each form holds exactly with smooth noise, so treat them as lower bounds.
- **Where the edge comes from.** It is a maximum over k and over groups. In practice it is the k = 4 track on tori with 3 | l. Fixed-k tracks give different exponents (0.61 to 0.70), so no single power law fits every k. A shared asymptotic d/sqrt(n) with a k-dependent offset is one consistent reading, but it is not established.
- **No theory pins the form.**
  - Wang and Pryadko (arXiv:2203.17216, Symmetry 2022) found that d ≈ A(w)·sqrt(n) + B(w) fits their exhaustive enumeration of k = 2 generalized bicycle codes at prime sizes.
  - They also give upper bounds by mapping these codes to codes local in a few dimensions (w − 2, from a search summary I did not check against the paper), and existence bounds of order sqrt(n).
  - So nothing proven forces sqrt(n), and these data cannot show that the codes outgrow sqrt(n) for good.
- **Data handling.**
  - The per-n maxima do not depend on duplicate isomorphic tori.
  - Class counts were deduplicated by group.
  - In my class counts (evt.py), the 9 stage-3d tori were set to d = 24 with counts taken from the 3d records.

angles.summary: Seen from the k direction, the scatter is regular because each extra logical qubit costs about one unit of distance, added on rather than multiplied in. At a given n, the per-(n,k) frontier is close to d ≈ D(n) − k: a set of roughly parallel bands, about 2 apart for each step of 2 in k. A 2-parameter surface d = 2.31·n^0.443 − k, fitted only on n ≤ 300, predicts the stage-4 frontier (n 306–384, 49 points) with RMS 2.0, and 94% of points land within one even step. The parameters barely move when it is fitted on n ≤ 200 instead. Even the 1-parameter d ≈ 1.69·√n − k does as well for k ≤ 16 (RMS 1.2, bias 0). It reproduces all eight band maxima of d/√n (1.155 → 1.488) to within 0.03, so the rising d/√n can be read as a finite-size offset (−4/√n from k = 4) with no log factor needed. The data cannot tell which function of n D(n) is: n^0.44, √n + 2, √(n ln n) + 5 and n^0.6 + 5 all predict stage 4 about equally well once the −k term is in. The BPT-type picture (k·d² ≈ S(k)·n, i.e. d ∝ k^−1/2) fits poorly. At every fixed k ≤ 16, k·d²/n still rises with n, the fitted per-k exponents rise from 0.68 (k = 4) to 1.18 (k = 16), and power-in-k surfaces miss stage 4 by 3.7–3.9 RMS. The '~14–16 bound' is just where the n ≤ 400 range ends. Inside single tori, d + k is nearly constant (median spread 4, coefficient of variation 7% vs 39% for k·d²), and a straight-line fall beats a power-law fall in 28 of 30 tori. Per-class data (n ≤ 200) show that about half of that drop is a real trade-off (the median class loses about 0.5 per unit k). The rest comes from the frontier being a maximum over fewer classes at larger k: about 120 classes at k = 4 against 2–3 at k ≥ 12. The top edge of the plot is always carried by the smallest k available at that n: the k = 4 staircase at multiples of 6, k = 6 at multiples of 14, and k = 10/16/18 at n divisible by 31/17/73. The fit breaks down for k ≥ 18 (degenerate d = 2–6 codes), for k = 16 on tori where 16 is the smallest k, and for the special published k = 12 codes on tori with 3 dividing both sides (the gross code +3, [[360,12,24]] +5), which sit above the surface.

angles.summary: The short answer: no theorem gives the shape of this curve, and the literature does not explain the regularity. The proven upper bound for weight-6 BB codes, and for any abelian two-block code, is d = O(n^{3/4}), not O(sqrt n). It works by treating each code as a geometrically local code in D = w − 2 = 4 dimensions. With its constants it says nothing for n < about 10^4. I found no proven O(sqrt n) bound for general weight-6 BB codes. The sqrt(n) barrier is proven only for the hypergraph-product subfamily (A in F2[x], B in F2[y]). On the lower side, families with d of order sqrt(n) provably exist (hypergraph products, and Wang-Pryadko's existence bound). No known construction beats sqrt(n) at fixed weight with an abelian group: n^{3/5} and n/log n codes, and asymptotically good codes, need a growing base matrix or non-abelian groups. The BPT bound k d^2 = O(n) does not apply. My stencil check shows the best census codes are not a fixed-stencil 2D-local family: their 2D stencil grows like N^{1/4}, just as random codes' does. So the flat-looking k d^2/n is an observation, not a consequence of any theorem. On the user's question, sqrt(n ln n) and a power law n^{0.61–0.64} differ in shape by only 1.7% over n = 50–400. The census cannot tell them apart, and they only separate by a step of d around n ≈ 1000–2000. Plain c·sqrt(n) and c·n^{3/4} both fit noticeably worse. Finally, the per-class data (stage 3a, n ≤ 200) do not support the idea that sqrt(n ln n) comes from taking a maximum over many classes. The mean, median and 90th percentile of d grow at the same rate as the maximum, and the best class sits only about 1.5 standard deviations above the mean however many classes there are. The frontier behaves like a ceiling that the bulk of codes presses against. Literature caveat: arxiv.org and mdpi.com were blocked, so every literature claim comes from web-search summaries, not full texts.
angles.results:
LABELS: [THM] = proven result in the cited source (read only through search summaries); [HEUR] = heuristic in the literature; [OWN] = my own reasoning or computation.

1. UPPER BOUNDS
- [THM] Wang & Pryadko, "Distance bounds for generalized bicycle codes", Symmetry 14, 1348 (2022), arXiv:2203.17216. For bounded weight w, GB codes map to codes that are local in D dimensions (the abstract says D ≤ w−1; an APS abstract says w−2), so the Bravyi-Terhal bound gives d = O(n^{(D−1)/D}). The paper also notes that GB codes with unrestricted weight can have linear distance.
- [THM] Arnault, Gaborit, Rozendaal, Saussay, Zémor, "A variant of the Bravyi-Terhal bound for arbitrary boundary conditions", arXiv:2502.04995 (cited elsewhere as IEEE TIT 72(1):437-446, 2026).
  - Statement: every non-trivial abelian 2BGA code of weight w is local with radius 1 on Z^D/Λ, D = w−2 (two qubits per vertex). Theorem 4.1, as quoted in search excerpts: d ≤ 2·sqrt(γ_D)·(sqrt(D)+4)·n^{(D−1)/D}, valid when n^{1/D} ≥ 8·sqrt(γ_D).
  - For w = 6: D = 4 and γ_4 = sqrt(2), so d ≤ 14.3·n^{3/4}. It applies only for n ≥ about 8,200, and it stays above n until n ≈ 41,000. It is vacuous for the census.
  - Whether n in the theorem counts qubits or group elements is unverified.
  - A third-party review site (pith.science) claims a gap in the lemma that reduces general 2BGA codes to this form. Unverified.
- [THM] Postema & Kokkelmans, arXiv:2502.17052 (2025): any constant-weight BB family is asymptotically bad (d/n → 0). The proof uses the generalised Bravyi-Terhal bound (their Thm 2.18/2.19).
- [THM] Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal, PRL 104, 050503 (2010), arXiv:0909.5200: k d^2 = O(n) needs 2D locality. The D-dimensional form is k d^{2/(D−1)} = O(n), which for D = 4 is k d^{2/3} = O(n) and does not bound k d^2/n.
  - Baspin & Krishna, Quantum 6, 711 (2022), arXiv:2106.00765: d is bounded by the separator of the connectivity graph. [OWN] For a 4D-like graph that again gives about n^{3/4}.
- [THM] Tillich & Zémor, IEEE TIT 60, 1193 (2014), arXiv:0903.0566: hypergraph products have d ≤ sqrt(n). This covers only BB codes with A = a(x), B = b(y). General BB codes are not hypergraph products.
- Not found: any proven O(sqrt n) bound for general weight-6 BB or abelian 2BGA codes.
- [OWN] Why the abelian setting limits distance: abelian Cayley graphs with a bounded number of generators have polynomial growth and are not expanders (cf. Alon & Roichman, Random Struct. Alg. 5 (1994) 271). Panteleev-Kalachev reach n/log n (arXiv:2012.04068, IEEE TIT 68 (2022) 213) with circulant size about N/log N, so their base matrix grows like log N, i.e. the effective D grows.

2. LOWER BOUNDS AND ACHIEVABILITY
- [THM, my application of the Tillich-Zémor formula] A = 1+x+x^2, B = 1+y+y^2 on an l x l torus with 3 | l is a hypergraph product with parameters [[2l^2, 8, 2l/3]], so d ≈ 0.47·sqrt(n). This proves Θ(sqrt n) for weight-6 BB codes, with a constant far below the census's 1.4–1.5.
- [THM] Wang-Pryadko (2022), per summary: GB codes with d = Ω(n^{1/2}) exist for every fixed w ≥ 4.
- [THM] arXiv:2504.18360 (GB codes generalising Kitaev's codes): [[2n, 2, ≥ sqrt n]] at weight 4.
- Codes that beat sqrt(n), none of them abelian with a fixed small base:
  - Freedman-Meyer-Luo (2002): sqrt(n)·log^{1/4} n.
  - Evra-Kaufman-Zémor, arXiv:2004.07935: sqrt(n)·log n.
  - Hastings-Haah-O'Donnell fiber bundle codes, arXiv:2009.03921: Ω(n^{3/5}/polylog).
  - Breuckmann-Eberhardt, arXiv:2012.09271.
  - Panteleev-Kalachev, arXiv:2012.04068 (n/log n) and arXiv:2111.03654 (good codes).
  - Leverrier-Zémor, arXiv:2202.13641.

3. PUBLISHED EMPIRICAL SCALING
- Wang-Pryadko 2022: exhaustive k = 2 GB enumerations at prime circulant sizes with w = 4, 6, 8 are "consistent with A(w)·n^{1/2} + B(w)", with A increasing in w. I could not retrieve the coefficients.
- I found no explicit fitted d-vs-n trend in:
  - Bravyi et al., Nature 627, 778 (2024), arXiv:2308.07915.
  - Lin-Pryadko, PRA 109, 022407 (2024), arXiv:2306.16400 (catalog n ≤ 100).
  - Wang-Mueller, arXiv:2408.10001 (Quantum 2026).
  - Liang et al., PRX Quantum 2025, arXiv:2503.03827 (tables to n ≤ 400; d > 20 are upper bounds).
  - Symons-Rajput-Browne, arXiv:2511.13560 (h-fold covers have d_h ≤ h·d for odd h, rarely saturated).
- Lee, "Bicycle Race", arXiv:2610.13880 (per its abstract): no weight-6 two-block code over any group with n ≤ 300 beats [[288,16,16]] (k d^2/n = 14.2).

4. OWN ANALYSIS OF THE CENSUS DATA (scripts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/8f17707b-68ac-58ba-8e5d-b4b134d43d3d/scratchpad/regularity/theory/)
(a) Extreme-value test (evt.py, evt2.py), on stage-3a per-class files in examples/qec-census-3/data. Sample: connected k = 4 classes with exact d, 37 groups after merging isomorphic tori, n = 42–198, M = 20 to 1,800 classes per group.
- Log-log slopes:
  - mean d ~ n^0.686
  - median d ~ n^0.708
  - 90th percentile ~ n^0.681
  - max d ~ n^0.670
  - standard deviation of d ~ n^0.498 (so SD/sqrt(n) ≈ 0.24, constant)
  - restricted to n ≥ 100: mean n^0.639, max n^0.666
- (max − mean)/SD averages 1.47, against a Gaussian expectation sqrt(2 ln M) averaging 3.19. Correlation of z with sqrt(2 ln M): r = 0.05, p = 0.77.
- A median 48% of classes lie within one even step of the maximum (range 12–75%). Example: 9x11 has 154 classes at d = 18 and 442 at d = 16.
- The highest step is sometimes reached by only 1 or 2 classes (3x28, 4x24, 5x9).
(b) 2D stencil diameter (rho2.py, rho2b.py): the minimum over maps Z^2 → G of the l∞ diameter of the embedded supports of A and B.
- The best code at each n grows from 2 (n ≤ 84) to 3 (n ≈ 90–250) to 4 (n ≥ 258).
- Random connected codes on the same tori, n = 270–384, give 2–6, typically 3–4. That is about N^{1/4}.
(c) Fits to the record points (first n reaching each d, n = 48–384, unweighted least squares):
  - c·sqrt(n): c = 1.369, rms 1.33, max residual 2.6 (systematic)
  - c·sqrt(n ln n): c = 0.587, rms 0.70, max 1.49
  - c·n^b: c = 0.632, b = 0.641, rms 0.60, max 1.18
  - c·n^{2/3}: c = 0.549, rms 0.63
  - sqrt(n)·(a + b ln n): a = 0.346, b = 0.187, rms 0.60
  - c·n^{3/4}: c = 0.346, rms 1.04, max 2.04
- sqrt(n ln n)/n^0.607 varies by only 1.7% over n = 50–400.
- The fitted sqrt(n ln n) and n^0.641 curves differ by 0.7 at n = 400, 4.3 at 1,000, 10.4 at 2,000 and 54 at 10^4.
(d) Best k d^2/n at fixed k, by 50-wide band, still rises:
  - k = 4: 5.3 → 8.9
  - k = 6: 5.1 → 12.4
  - k = 8: 4.3 → 14.1
  - k = 10: 3.8 → 15.6
  No theorem bounds it. If d ∝ n^0.64 at fixed k, then k d^2/n ∝ n^0.28.
(e) [OWN, speculative] In the D = 4 picture the torus has linear size L = (n/2)^{1/4} ≈ 2.5–3.7 for n ≤ 384, deep in the pre-asymptotic regime. Asymptotically, theory allows exponents between 1/2 (the construction lower bound) and 3/4 (Bravyi-Terhal). The observed 0.61–0.69 lies inside that window.

- Literature access was limited. arxiv.org and www.mdpi.com do not resolve in this session; they would have to be allowed in the session's network settings to read the full papers. Every literature statement above comes from web-search summaries written by a model, not from page text. That includes the constants and validity condition of Arnault et al. Theorem 4.1, whether its n counts qubits or group elements, and the D ≤ w−1 vs w−2 discrepancy in Wang-Pryadko.
- A search summary cited a "Hopkins et al." for a BPT bound on BB codes. I could not find that paper and did not use it.
- I did not retrieve the Wang-Pryadko fitted coefficient A(6).
- A third-party review claims a gap in Arnault et al.'s reduction lemma; it is unverified.
- The 2D stencil diameter is my own diagnostic: l-infinity triangle diameter, box radius 7, only 6 random codes per torus as a baseline.
- The extreme-value test uses only stage 3a (n ≤ 200) and only k = 4 connected classes. It treats classes as units, but classes are an upper bound on inequivalent codes.
- d is quantised in steps of 2, so per-torus distributions take only 3–8 distinct values; the qualitative conclusion holds despite this.
- The exponents (0.64–0.70) come from n ≤ 200 for the class bulk and n ≤ 384 for the frontier. They are pre-asymptotic and should not be extrapolated.
- Stage 4 is about 75% complete. 10 entries (for example 3x45 at n = 270) have no polynomials and were skipped in the stencil computation.
- The "4D torus of linear size (n/2)^{1/4}" reading and the 1/2-to-3/4 exponent window are my reasoning, not a published result.
